rationale: A wins because it stays inside the evidence and turns the weak spots into proof gates instead of theater. Its best angle, "Flat fee vs. interchange: the math behind Plaid's \"up to 70% cheaper\" claim," is a real reporter assignment with a real kill condition. B has useful bones, but "FedNow just got its most significant commercial test" is the kind of unsupported superlative that gets a founder into trouble before the first reply.
gaps_in_A: "FedNow gets a merchant-facing on-ramp through Plaid's 12,000 bank connections" risks implying all 12,000 institutions are FedNow-reachable; A asks the right proof question later, but the headline should not outrun the fact.
"Flat fee vs. interchange" misses one obvious comparison a payments reporter will ask: ACH and same-day ACH pricing, not just card interchange.

"a Plaid spokesperson willing to say plainly that this competes with card interchange" is a useful ask, but too binary; the structural competition can still be reported even if Plaid refuses to say the quiet part out loud.
gaps_in_B: "FedNow just got its most significant commercial test" is invented altitude. The update says Pay by Bank uses FedNow rails; it does not prove this is FedNow's biggest commercial test.
"Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes. Now it wants to own the payment." imports company-history and intent that were not in the supplied facts.
"competing simultaneously with Stripe and Adyen" is unsupported competitor framing. Plaid may compete with processors, but this update only gives card-network bypass and merchant fees.
"Merchants using Plaid's Pay by Bank report fees up to 70% lower" overstates the evidence. The update says Plaid says early merchants see that figure, and no named merchant is on record.
